The clinical summary presents a classic presentation of disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) manifesting as septic arthritis — specifically, acute septic arthritis of the left wrist. Key diagnostic anchors include: (1) acute onset of monoarticular joint pain with systemic symptoms (chills, malaise) and no trauma; (2) peripheral leukocytosis (WBC 15,000/μL), consistent with systemic infection; (3) synovial fluid with purulent effusion (WBC >50,000/μL), confirming septic arthritis; and most critically, (4) Gram stain showing intracellular gram-negative diplococci — which, in the context of an acute inflammatory monoarthritis in a sexually active individual, is highly specific for *Neisseria gonorrhoeae*. While other gram-negative diplococci (e.g., *Moraxella catarrhalis*) exist, they are exceedingly rare in synovial fluid and not associated with this clinical syndrome. The absence of trauma, rapid progression, and demographic plausibility further support gonococcal etiology over non-gonococcal bacterial septic arthritis (e.g., *Staphylococcus aureus*), which more commonly occurs post-trauma or in immunocompromised hosts and rarely shows intracellular diplococci on Gram stain. Pending imaging and inflammatory markers (CRP, ESR) do not alter the high pretest probability established by the pathognomonic Gram stain finding + clinical triad (acute monoarthritis, systemic symptoms, leukocytosis). Thus, the diagnosis is definitive at the microbiologic–clinical level.

- Acute onset of localized left wrist pain without trauma  
- Systemic symptoms including chills and malaise  
- Peripheral leukocytosis (WBC 15,000/μL)  
- Synovial fluid WBC >50,000/μL (purulent effusion)
